body.observations: Default run r001 (weightUdp=0.5, queuePkts=100, TcpCubic, duration=10, seed=1) gives udp_goodput_bps=300003200, udp_loss_frac=0.0, tcp_goodput_bps=482667053, drops_band1=77, tcp_retrans=77, link_util=0.807098. The TCP goodput is almost exactly 0.5*1e9*(1448/1500)=482666667 bps, i.e. TCP appears to receive exactly its configured wire share (500 Mbps wire) and payload is 1448/1500 of wire bits. If TCP wire is 500 Mbps, the remaining transmitted wire bits implied by link_util are about 307.1 Mbps, suggesting UDP's wire demand is slightly above its 300 Mbps payload rate, roughly 307 Mbps. The unused UDP share at weightUdp=0.5 is not used by TCP, so the scheduler may be strict weighted fair rather than work-conserving.

body.text: UDP's wire demand is slightly above 300 Mbps (about 307 Mbps), so weightUdp=0.30 is below demand and causes more than 1% UDP loss over a 10s measured window, while weightUdp=0.32 is above demand and keeps UDP loss at or below 1%.

With queuePkts=1000: w=0.30 has udp_loss_frac=0.017841 and tcp_goodput_bps=666522080; w=0.305 has udp_loss_frac=0.0 and tcp_goodput_bps=661752557; w=0.31 has tcp_goodput_bps=658547917 and link_util=0.997641; for w>=0.31, tcp_goodput_bps is very close to 954.417*(1-w) Mbps, and link_util is below 1 when UDP demand is below the configured UDP share. Thus the scheduler does not lend idle UDP share to TCP in the large-queue idle-UDP case, but small queues can change TCP throughput near the UDP-demand boundary. Checks C1 and C2 both held.

body.text: With queuePkts=1000, the UDP loss constraint allows weightUdp as low as about 0.301, and TCP goodput increases as weightUdp is decreased in this range.

For the same weightUdp near the UDP-demand boundary, a smaller scheduler queue (100 packets instead of 1000 packets) can increase TCP goodput by more than 5 Mbps while still keeping UDP loss at or below 1%, because UDP queue emptying/dropping lets TCP use some of the UDP-configured share.

body.observations: The ledger shows a strict weighted-fair scheduler (V1) and that UDP's wire demand is just above 0.30 of the link (V2). With queuePkts=1000, weightUdp=0.303 gives udp_loss_frac=0.00706 and tcp_goodput_bps=663661024 (r018), but the series shows a very large TCP queue (about 946 packets) and cwnd near 1 MB, indicating bufferbloat. With queuePkts=100 at the same weight, udp_loss_frac=0.009815 and tcp_goodput_bps=671532589 (r022), about 7.87 Mbps higher, with much smaller TCP queue/cwnd. queuePkts=10 gives the same UDP loss and TCP goodput as queuePkts=100 but many more TCP drops/retransmissions (r025 vs r022). The current best seed-1 candidate is weightUdp=0.303, queuePkts=100, but its UDP loss is only 0.000185 below the 1% limit, so seed robustness is uncertain. weightUdp=0.3035 has not been measured, and weightUdp=0.304 has seed-1 udp_loss_frac=0.006544 and tcp_goodput_bps=670567642 (r023). The open questions are whether weightUdp=0.303 is feasible across seeds 2-4, whether 0.3035/0.304 are robust, and whether queue sizes 50/200/400 can beat queuePkts=100 by more than 1 Mbps while feasible.

C12 measured udp_loss_frac=0.009658 and tcp_goodput_bps=671628736 at weightUdp=0.3029, queuePkts=400, TcpCubic, duration=10, seed=1, so H12's prediction held. Across the ledger, the feasible TCP-goodput frontier is controlled by the UDP scheduler share: TCP goodput falls roughly linearly as weightUdp increases, while UDP loss rises as weightUdp falls. At queuePkts=400, weightUdp=0.3028 is just infeasible (udp_loss_frac=0.010016), while weightUdp=0.3029 is feasible and gives the highest tested TCP goodput. queuePkts=400 matches the TCP goodput of queuePkts=100 at weightUdp=0.303 but has lower UDP loss and far fewer TCP drops/retransmissions, and it avoids the TCP-goodput penalty seen with queuePkts=1000. TcpBbr was feasible at weightUdp=0.303 but used only about 0.728 of the link and gave much lower TCP goodput than TcpCubic.

body.explanation: The scheduler behaves as a strict weighted-fair scheduler for the configured shares: when UDP demand is below weightUdp, TCP does not receive the unused UDP share, so TCP goodput is approximately (1-weightUdp) times the link rate scaled by TCP payload overhead. This is shown by the default and weightUdp=0.35 runs, where link_util is UDP wire demand plus the configured TCP share rather than near 1.0. UDP's required scheduler share is just below 0.303 for the fixed 300 Mbps UDP payload load: at queuePkts=400, weightUdp=0.3028 gives udp_loss_frac=0.010016, violating the constraint, while weightUdp=0.3029 gives udp_loss_frac=0.009658 and tcp_goodput_bps=671628736, the highest TCP goodput tested under the constraint. queuePkts=400 is the best tested queue size because it reaches the same TCP goodput as queuePkts=100 at weightUdp=0.303 (671532589 bps) but reduces UDP loss from 0.009815 to 0.0093 and TCP drops/retransmissions from 91 to 7, while queuePkts=1000 gives much lower TCP goodput at the same weight. TcpBbr was tested at the same feasible point and was feasible but far worse for TCP goodput (409658893 bps, link_util=0.728358), so TcpCubic is the best tested TCP variant. The recommended point therefore sits just on the feasible side of the UDP-loss boundary, where TCP receives almost all of its configured share and the link is fully utilized.
body.holds_when: The fixed system parameters remain unchanged: 1 Gbps link, 50 us one-way delay, 1500-byte MTU, UDP application sending 1400-byte packets at 300 Mbps payload, TCP always backlogged, 1 MB TCP buffers, 10-packet device queue, and the observed strict weighted-fair scheduler behavior. The recommendation is measured for duration=10 and seed=1; nearby seeds tested at the adjacent point weightUdp=0.303, queuePkts=100 showed very small seed variation, but seed robustness at exactly 0.3029, queuePkts=400 was not directly tested.
body.breaks_when: If the UDP offered load increases, the feasible weightUdp threshold rises and 0.3029 would violate udp_loss_frac <= 0.01. If scheduler behavior changes to work-conserving lending of idle UDP share, the optimum weightUdp could be lower. If seed or duration changes move UDP loss above 0.01 at 0.3029, use weightUdp=0.303 with queuePkts=400, which has more margin and only about 0.096 Mbps lower TCP goodput in the tested seed. If another TCP variant not tested here (TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpVegas, or TcpBic) outperforms TcpCubic, the TCP variant recommendation could change.

claims.text: The scheduler does not lend idle UDP share to TCP; TCP goodput tracks the configured TCP share when UDP demand is below weightUdp.
At queuePkts=400, the UDP-loss boundary for the fixed UDP load lies between weightUdp=0.3028 and weightUdp=0.3029.

queuePkts=400 is better than queuePkts=100 and queuePkts=1000 at the boundary: it matches queuePkts=100 TCP goodput while reducing UDP loss and TCP drops, and avoids the TCP-goodput penalty of queuePkts=1000.
TcpCubic outperforms TcpBbr for this goal at the tested feasible settings.
The highest tested feasible TCP goodput is obtained with weightUdp=0.3029, queuePkts=400, TcpCubic, duration=10, seed=1.

open_questions: The exact optimum between weightUdp=0.3028 and 0.3029 was not tested; the true feasible maximum may be slightly above 671628736 bps.
Other TCP variants (TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpVegas, TcpBic) were not tested against TcpCubic.
Seed robustness at exactly weightUdp=0.3029, queuePkts=400 was not directly tested, although adjacent points showed very small seed sensitivity.
Queue sizes between 400 and 1000 were not fully explored; queuePkts=400 is best among tested values but not proven globally optimal.
